newsitem.title: USA: No quick fix seen on U.S. CPI mismeasurement.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix seen on U.S. CPI mismeasurement.

text.p: An upcoming report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics will sharpen the debate on fixing the consumer price index, but inflation experts say any change is likely to occur gradually over several years.

In the next few days the Joint Economic Committee of Congress will release a BLS study which directly responds to findings of a Congressionally-commissioned panel headed by Stanford University professor Michael Boskin.
Analysts cited doubts over Boskin's conclusion that CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points annually and called for the BLS to continue upgrading the index in installments.
"I'm still skeptical about whether the bias has really been 1.1 percent," said Paul Armknecht, who served as BLS assistant commissioner for consumer prices from 1988 to 1995.

"The (Boskin) commission used examples that did not necessarily represent full coverage across the scheme of consumer products and made some heroic assumptions about those changes," added Armknecht, now a consultant to the International Monetary Fund.
Boskin was not immediately available for comment.
While details of the BLS study are not yet known, the response could go a long way toward shaping the debate over improving the CPI.
"Our position is one of wanting more information," said JEC executive director Chris Frenze. "Up to now the whole debate has really been framed by one group of people.
The BLS has already made minor adjustments to the CPI that should give a more accurate 1997 reading than in 1996, economists said.

"My impression is that while (BLS) were not necessarily enthusiastic about the Boskin commission's reported recommendations, they have gone quietly about their business of trying to improve the statistics," said Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis President Gary Stern at a conference in Milwaukee on Wednesday.

Congress has declined to legislate CPI changes and spurned proposals to include a scaled-back index for setting federal benefits and tax brackets in the historic balanced-budget framework reached this spring.
"It's one of those issues that I hope people would be prepared to move on, but I must say that it seems to have dropped from the agenda, at least as I read the press these days," said Stern.
The House this year overwhelmingly passed a resolution calling on the BLS to resolve the CPI issue itself.
"It would seem that rather than making an ad hoc legislative adjustment, leaving it to the BLS to make the adjustment has made sense to us since the Boskin commission report came out," said Frenze.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has proposed an independent board that would annually determine the amount CPI overstated inflation for purposes of calculating federal entitlements and tax payments.
In the meantime, the BLS has devised an experimental CPI, which showed inflation rose 2.9 percent in 1996, less than the official CPI increase of 3.3 percent.
The new index uses a geometric rather than an arithmetic mean to account for consumers switching to new products when prices on similar goods rise, eliminating the so-called substitution bias.

While analysts agreed with the Boskin finding that the substitution bias adds about 0.5 percentage points to CPI annually, they disputed the assertion that mismeasuring quality improvements and new goods adds another 0.6 points.
"I don't know if I believe the amount of the bias that the commission came up with. That's an area that needs considerably more research," said Armknecht.
That research could take several more years and ideally would continue indefinitely to keep the CPI in step with an ever-changing economy, analysts said.

"A number of factors will have to be taken into account. The geometric mean is only one factor moving us closer to a true cost-of-living index," said Joel Popkin, another former BLS assistant commissioner who helped design the CPI.
